Catalysis is a fundamental process in chemistry that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, without the catalyst being consumed in the process. The term "catalyst" derives from Greek ÎºÎ±ÏÎ±Î»ÏÎµÎ¹Î½ (kataluein), meaning "to loosen" or "to untie." The concept of catalysis was first explored by chemist Elizabeth Fulhame in 1794 through her work on oxidation-reduction reactions.
 In chemical reactions, reactants transform into products by breaking and forming chemical bonds. This process requires overcoming an energy barrier called activation energy. Catalysts facilitate this transformation by lowering this energy barrier, making it easier for atoms to recombine and form new substances. The catalyst participates in the reaction by forming temporary intermediates with reactants but is regenerated at the end of the reaction cycle. This is why catalysts can be used repeatedly and in small amounts relative to the reactants.
 Catalysis is categorized into three main types: homogeneous, heterogeneous, and biocatalysis. In homogeneous catalysis, the catalyst exists in the same phase as the reactants, typically dissolved in a solution. Examples include acid catalysis in esterification reactions. Heterogeneous catalysis involves the catalyst and reactants in different phases, commonly with solid catalysts interacting with gaseous or liquid reactants. Industrial processes frequently employ heterogeneous catalysts due to ease of separation and recovery. Biocatalysis utilizes enzymes, nature's specialized protein catalysts, to accelerate biochemical reactions with remarkable efficiency and specificity.
 The mechanism of catalytic action varies but generally involves several steps: adsorption of reactants onto the catalyst, activation of reactants through bond weakening, reaction between activated species, and desorption of products, which regenerates the catalyst. This cycle can occur millions of times for a single catalyst molecule, explaining the high efficiency of catalytic processes.

scenario.title: Domino Cascade: The Catalyst Effect
scenario.content: Students will explore catalysis through a digital domino setup where regular dominoes (reactant molecules) can only fall at a slow rate due to their spacing (energy barrier). Special golden dominoes (catalysts) can be strategically placed to create temporary bridges or alternative pathways that allow the cascade to proceed much faster. Students observe and analyze how these special pieces remain unchanged after the reaction completes and can be reused for multiple domino cascades.

hypothesis.description: Students will be able to explain how catalysts increase reaction rates by providing alternative reaction pathways with lower activation energy, and demonstrate understanding that catalysts are not consumed during reactions, allowing them to participate in multiple reaction cycles without being depleted.
